summary: `identity.handle` and each entry of `topics` ride the presence beat, whose decoder enforces MAX_HANDLE_LEN (128) and MAX_TOPIC_LEN (512), but the config schema bounds neither. A config past either limit loads cleanly and is then discarded by every peer, forever, with no error anywhere.
failure: `parseConfig({ identity: { handle: 'h'.repeat(129) }, topics: ['ctx'] })` loads. startPresenceLoop posts `{handle: <129 chars>, ...}`; every reader's decodePresence hits `if (handle.length > MAX_HANDLE_LEN) return null` (engine/presence-beat.ts:142) and drops the WHOLE beat — the bridge never appears in any peer's parley_list_users. One axis over: `topics: ['t'.repeat(513)]` loads, and `decodePresence(...).topics === []`, so the bridge is never advertised as reachable on that topic. Reproduced in a probe test; both assertions passed.
remediation: In config.ts bound `identity.handle` with `.max(MAX_HANDLE_LEN)` and each `topics`/`post_topics` element with `.max(MAX_TOPIC_LEN)`, importing the constants from engine/presence-beat.ts exactly as `topics`'s existing `.max(MAX_RECORD_TOPICS)` does, with the same rationale in the message. Derive the message text from the constants so raising a wire cap re-grades the loader.
testUpgrade: config.test.ts's `describe('a config list carried by the presence beat is capped where it is declared')` closes only the COUNT axis. Widen it to every CONFIG VALUE the beat carries, on both axes: enumerate the PresenceRecord fields the real emitter populates (it already does this via Object.entries(beat)); for each derive the config path feeding it and every cap decodePresence applies — count, per-element length, and whole-record-reject length — then assert the three-way verdict `refused at load | carried in full | truncated on the wire` at cap and cap+1, with `truncated on the wire` and `record dropped` both illegal. A new capped field, or a new cap on an existing field, then fails as a missing row rather than passing silently.

summary: The ReDoS screen's exponential-signature test is `body && quantMax >= 2`, and its doc pins the boundary exactly ("a bounded count >= 2 is as catastrophic as an unbounded one; only a bound of <= 1 cannot compound"). No corpus row uses a repeat count of 2 — the smallest is `{8}` — so the boundary is never graded, and this guard is the security control behind operator-supplied `post_topics`.
failure: Change line 152 to `if (body && quantMax > 2) return false;`. All 44 core test files / 2721 tests stay green (measured). The mutant then accepts `(?:[a-z]*[a-z]*[a-z]*[a-z]*){2}`: isRedosSafeSource returns true, `parseConfig({ post_topics: [that] })` loads, and a single `Allowlist.has('a'.repeat(40) + '!')` — a 41-char topic, well under MAX_MATCH_INPUT — blocks the event loop for 17,006 ms. One parley_post call from a prompt-injected agent wedges the bridge.
remediation: Keep the code as-is; close the grading hole. Add boundary rows to testing/regex-corpus.ts: `['ambiguous group at the smallest compounding repeat', '(?:a|aa){2}']` and `['risky body at the smallest compounding repeat', '(?:[a-z]*[a-z]*[a-z]*[a-z]*){2}']` to HOSTILE_PATTERNS; `['ambiguous group at the non-compounding bound', '(?:a|aa){1}']` and `['ambiguous group made optional', '(?:a|aa)?']` to SAFE_PATTERNS.
testUpgrade: Guard the CLASS "a documented inequality in a screen is graded only strictly inside its region", the way stated-bounds.test.ts already does for capacities: generate the corpus along the repeat-count axis parametrically — for n in {1,2,3,8,250} emit `(?:a|aa){n}` and `(?:[a-z]*[a-z]*[a-z]*[a-z]*){n}` and assert refusal exactly for n >= 2, with the pivot derived from the code's own constant rather than a literal. Additionally extend regex-safety.test.ts's timing case from CORPUS to every ACCEPTED source in ALL_CANDIDATES (it already builds 40k and times ~90), so a future accept-side leak is caught by cost rather than by having guessed the shape.

summary: `include: ["src/**/*"]` with no test exclude means `tsc -b` (run by prepublishOnly) compiles every `*.test.ts` and the whole `src/testing/` fixture tree into dist/, and `files: ["dist"]` publishes them. bridge-sqlite already carries the fix (`"exclude": ["src/**/*.test.ts"]`); bridge-core does not.
failure: `npx tsc -b packages/bridge-core && npm pack -w @sharptrick/parley-core --dry-run` → 378 files, 422.8 kB packed / 1.8 MB unpacked, including 44 `dist/**/*.test.js` (e.g. dist/auth/keycloak.e2e.test.js) plus dist/testing/fake-oidc.js, dist/testing/fake-plugin.js, dist/testing/tool-harness.js. Every dist/**/*.test.js carries `import ... from 'vitest'`, which is in neither this package's dependencies nor devDependencies — a resolvable-but-unloadable module in the published artifact, and roughly half the tarball is dead weight.
remediation: Add `"exclude": ["src/**/*.test.ts"]` to packages/bridge-core/tsconfig.json, matching bridge-sqlite. Decide deliberately about src/testing/: nothing outside bridge-core's own tests imports it (verified by grep across all packages), so either exclude it too, or give it an `"./testing"` entry in `exports` and declare the intent.
testUpgrade: bridge-redis/bridge-postgres already carry test/packaging.test.ts grading the manifest's promises, but it is keyed to its own package directory and can never see bridge-core. Add the mirror rule and give bridge-core the test: for every public workspace package, assert no path the `files` globs would ship matches `**/*.test.*`, and that every shipped dist module's imports resolve to a declared dependency. Derive the package set from scripts/lib/workspaces.mjs rather than a hand list, so a package added later is graded on arrival.

summary: `"license": "MIT"` with `files: ["dist"]` and no LICENSE file beside package.json. npm packs LICENSE only from the package directory, so the published tarball declares MIT and carries no licence text.
failure: `ls packages/bridge-core/` → README.md, package.json, src, tsconfig.json (no LICENSE). `npm pack -w @sharptrick/parley-core --dry-run | grep -i license` → no match, while packages/bridge-redis/LICENSE exists. A consumer running a licence scanner over the core tarball sees an unlicensed artifact. Only 4 of 13 packages have a LICENSE at all.

Hoist it to a repo-level case parameterized over publicWorkspaces() — the class is "a manifest promise only a per-package file keeps", and the guard must be keyed to the package SET, never to one package's own path.

summary: The `Cursor` JSDoc — which ships verbatim in dist/message.d.ts and is the specification an out-of-tree plugin author reads — says core "never parses, COMPARES, or sorts by cursor value". Core does compare: catchUpTopic uses `nextCursor === since` as its no-progress brake. seam.ts states the corrected version and adds the obligation the false doc omits.
failure: engine/catchup.ts:71 `if (messages.length === 0 || nextCursor === since) return total;`. seam.ts:12-14 says "it does compare two for byte equality, as the no-progress brake in catchUpTopic. A cursor naming a position must therefore be byte-stable across calls." A plugin author reading only Cursor's doc is licensed to mint a non-byte-stable cursor for the same position (one embedding a fetch timestamp or a nonce). That plugin then defeats the brake: a full page whose cursor never semantically advances but is never byte-equal pages until MAX_PAGES, on every catch-up, forever — the exact shape testing/nonconformant.ts's 'a full page whose cursor never advances' exists to bound.
remediation: Rewrite the Cursor doc to state the actual contract and the obligation it puts on a plugin: core never parses, orders or sorts a cursor, but it does compare two for byte equality, so a cursor naming a position must be byte-stable across calls. State it once and have the other site point at it, so the two cannot drift again.
testUpgrade: index.test.ts already derives doc-vs-code offenders rather than naming them; extend that machinery to CONTRADICTION between shipped docs and code on one contract. Enumerate the verbs core actually applies to a cursor by scanning src/** for cursor-typed comparisons (`=== since`, `<`, `.sort(`), and assert that no barrel-exported symbol's JSDoc contains a negation of a verb the code performs (a small verb table: parse/compare/sort/order). That guards the class "a public doc denies a behaviour the package relies on" rather than this one sentence.

summary: The `shipped JSDoc never links a value the barrel withholds` guard attaches a JSDoc block only to the immediately-following TOP-LEVEL export declaration, so member-level JSDoc inside an exported interface or class is never scanned. A live offender already sits behind the hole.
failure: AllowlistOptions.postPatterns (allowlist.ts:46-54) documents "the collection is capped at {@link MAX_POST_TOPICS}" and AllowlistOptions is barrel-exported, so the link ships in dist/allowlist.d.ts. index.ts does not export MAX_POST_TOPICS. Verified by probe: `'MAX_POST_TOPICS' in api === false` while allowlist.ts contains `{@link MAX_POST_TOPICS}`, and the guard is green. An embedder who builds an Allowlist by hand — the exact caller that option's doc addresses — is told the cap's name and cannot import it, so they hardcode 64.
remediation: Either export MAX_POST_TOPICS from index.ts (it is already documented as public-facing) or restate the cap in prose. Then fix the scanner: attach a doc block to the nearest following declaration line including interface and class members, not only lines matching EXPORT_DECL, and treat an exported container's members as part of its public doc.
testUpgrade: Guard the class "the scanner's reach is narrower than the surface it claims to grade" by giving the scanner negative controls, exactly as source-hygiene.test.ts does for its lints: a fires/passes table of synthetic snippets — a top-level export with a bad link, an INTERFACE MEMBER with a bad link, a CLASS METHOD with a bad link, a member with a good link — asserted against the extraction function directly. A scanner that cannot see a shape then fails as a red control rather than as a clean run.

summary: `CAPACITY_MODULES = ['config.ts', 'identity-filter.ts', 'regex-safety.ts', 'topic-name.ts']` is a hand-kept literal, while the comment beside it claims "The modules are scanned, so a capacity added to any of them needs a row here rather than arriving unpinned." A capacity exported from any other module is unpinned and nothing notices — CLAUDE.md's standing rule asks for a glob over src/** here, not a file list.
failure: Adding `export const MAX_UNPINNED_CAP = 7;` to allowlist.ts leaves stated-bounds.test.ts, index.test.ts and allowlist.test.ts fully green (277 tests). Adding the same line to regex-safety.ts correctly reddens — proving the guard works only for the four listed files. Live instances already exist: engine/presence-beat.ts exports MAX_RECORD_TOPICS, MAX_INSTANCE_ID_LEN, MAX_HANDLE_LEN, MAX_TOPIC_LEN, MAX_CLOCK_SKEW_MS and engine/presence.ts exports MAX_HANDLE_INSTANCES, MAX_ROSTER_ENTRIES; grep finds no test pinning any of their VALUES. MAX_HANDLE_LEN and MAX_TOPIC_LEN are the two constants behind the first finding in this report.
remediation: Replace the literal with a recursive walk of src/**/*.ts (excluding *.test.ts), keeping the same `^export const ((?:MAX|MIN|DEFAULT)_[A-Z0-9_]+)` scan, and add the missing CAPACITIES rows for the engine constants. Keep an `expect(scanned.length).toBeGreaterThan(N)` control so a broken walk cannot read as a clean repository.
testUpgrade: This is the class "a guard that reads as derived but is keyed to a hand-kept layout list". Cover it durably by making every such registry in the suite derive its inputs from a src/** glob plus a non-vacuity floor, and add one shared meta-case asserting each registry's scanned-input count exceeds that floor — so a registry that silently narrows (a renamed file, a moved module) fails as a red control instead of as coverage that no longer covers anything.

summary: OidcTokenVerifier's class doc states `iss`, `exp`/`nbf` ± skew and `aud` are ALWAYS enforced, but jose only validates `exp` when the claim is present. A JWT with no `exp` passes verification and returns an AuthInfo with no `expiresAt`. The 401 that eventually results comes from the SDK's requireBearerAuth, not from this class, and carries the SDK's own distinct message — defeating the REJECTION_MESSAGE invariant three lines above it, which exists precisely so 'a caller cannot tell which check refused it'. The shared fake (src/testing/fake-oidc.ts:91) always calls setExpirationTime, so no test can reach the class.
failure: Mint an RS256 JWT with correct kid/iss/aud/sub, `iat` ten years ago and NO `exp`. Direct: `new OidcTokenVerifier({issuer, audience, jwksUri, allowedSubjects:['owner-sub']}).verifyAccessToken(tok)` RESOLVES with `{clientId:'x'}` and `expiresAt === undefined` (reproduced). End to end through createOidcRemoteApp: POST /mcp with that bearer -> 401 `WWW-Authenticate: Bearer error="invalid_token", error_description="Token has no expiration time"`, while the SAME token minted with sub='stranger' (fails the identity gate) -> 401 `error_description="invalid or expired access token"`, as does a garbage bearer. A caller therefore learns, from the message alone, that their signature, iss, aud AND the identity gate all passed — the exact disclosure REJECTION_MESSAGE was written to prevent, and a differential that enumerates the allowed_subjects/usernames policy.
remediation: Enforce the claim in the verifier rather than downstream: pass `requiredClaims: ['exp','iat']` (or at minimum `['exp']`) to jwtVerify, so an exp-less token is refused inside the try/catch that normalises every failure to REJECTION_MESSAGE. Then either always populate `expiresAt` or assert it is a number before returning, so requireBearerAuth's distinct 'Token has no expiration time' branch is unreachable. Fix the class doc to say what is enforced.
testUpgrade: The CLASS is 'a claim the verifier's contract says it enforces is absent from the token, so the check silently does not run, and the refusal that does happen carries a distinguishable message'. Two ratchets, both parameterized: (a) widen src/testing/fake-oidc.ts's FakeOidcClaims with an `omit?: Array<'exp'|'nbf'|'iat'|'iss'|'aud'|'sub'>` knob and drive a table over every omittable claim x {verifier accepts?, message}, asserting every rejection is byte-identical to REJECTION_MESSAGE; (b) an end-to-end table over a corpus of malformed/deficient bearers (garbage, bad signature, wrong iss, wrong aud, expired, nbf-future, gate-failing, exp-less, iat-less) asserting `new Set(responses.map(r => r.error_description)).size === 1` for every 401. The existing oidc-verifier tests are too narrow because every mint path in the repo hard-codes setExpirationTime.

summary: `authorize()` caps `pending` with `shedOldest`, which is pure insertion-order FIFO. The provider already models the distinction that matters — `clientStates()` yields pending consents as `ownerApproved: false`, and `evictionCandidate` uses that tier to protect the `clients` map — but none of it is applied to `pending` itself. MAX_PENDING is 100 and the SDK's /authorize limiter is 100 per 15 min per address, so one anonymous caller's full quota is exactly enough to flush the map. eviction.ts's module doc claims shedding was chosen so the anonymous filler 'cannot lock the owner out of the only path that authorizes the bridge'; for `pending`, shedding IS the lockout.
failure: Reproduced: owner opens /authorize (one PendingConsent recorded). An attacker registers one client via open DCR and issues 100 /authorize calls with that client_id. `pending.size === 100`, `pending.has(ownerConsentId) === false`, and `provider.completeConsent(ownerConsentId, <the correct owner passphrase>)` rejects with `ConsentError: consent request expired or unknown`. Repeatable every 15 minutes from a single address, and immediately from several — the owner can never complete a consent while the flood runs.
remediation: Give the pending cap the same two-tier policy the client cap already has: instead of `shedOldest`, evict the oldest entry belonging to the client_id that currently holds the MOST pending consents (equivalently, cap pending per client_id at ceil(MAX_PENDING/N)), so a single flooding registration can never displace a consent belonging to a different client. Reuse/extend `evictionCandidate` rather than adding a second policy, so the two caps cannot drift.
testUpgrade: The CLASS is 'an anonymous caller filling a capped store displaces state the OWNER is mid-way through creating'. Add a parameterized table over every capped store the provider keeps — {store, how an anonymous caller adds an entry, how the owner adds one, cap constant} — with one row per store asserting: after the owner creates its entry and an anonymous caller adds `cap` entries, the owner's entry is still present AND still usable (completeConsent succeeds / getClient returns it). Today only the `clients` row exists (oauth-provider.test.ts:1071 'the DCR cap never evicts a client that is in use'); the `pending` row is missing, which is why the mutation 'drop shedOldest' is caught while 'shed the owner's consent' is not.

summary: The guard that closes round 2's `self-skipping-e2e-on-a-reachability-probe` asserts only that a test file which mentions `describe.skip|describe.skipIf|it.skip` ALSO contains the substring `process.env.` somewhere in the file. It never inspects the expression the skip is actually gated on. keycloak.e2e.test.ts contains `process.env.PARLEY_KEYCLOAK_URL` on line 12 unconditionally, so the assertion is satisfied no matter what the skip reads — the guard is vacuous against precisely the regression it was written to catch, while counting as coverage.
failure: Mutation: replace `const OPTED_OUT = process.env.PARLEY_E2E === '0';` (keycloak.e2e.test.ts:21) with `const OPTED_OUT = await fetch('http://127.0.0.1:1/probe').then(() => false).catch(() => true);` — i.e. skip the whole suite on a runtime reachability probe. Result: `hygiene.test.ts (29 tests) PASSED`, `keycloak.e2e.test.ts (1 test | 1 skipped)`. Twelve real e2e assertions became one skipped placeholder and the ratchet stayed green.
remediation: Assert the guarded EXPRESSION, not the file: extract the condition text of each `describe.skipIf(...)` / `it.skipIf(...)` and of any `if (...)` whose consequent contains `describe.skip`, then require that expression to match `process\.env\.\w+` and to contain none of `fetch(`, `await `, `connect`, `ping`. Stronger and location-independent: run each `*.e2e.test.ts` as a child vitest process with its opt-out env unset and its dependency host pointed at an unreachable port, and assert a NON-ZERO exit — that grades the behaviour instead of the text.
testUpgrade: The CLASS is 'a structural guard whose assertion is satisfied by text elsewhere in the file rather than by the construct under test'. Make every such guard self-verifying the way BANNED_COMMENT_SHAPES already is: pair each structural rule with a table of SYNTHETIC OFFENDER sources (here: a file that both mentions `process.env.X` and gates its skip on a probe) and assert the rule REJECTS each one, alongside the existing table asserting it accepts the real sources. That mutation-proofs the ratchet itself and generalises to the other two structural scanners in this file.

summary: `assertOptionsMatchMode` exists because 'An option the selected mode never forwards is a silent no-op', and it refuses stray entries of the `opts` object at boot. The same rule is not applied to `cfg`: under `auth.mode: 'builtin'` the entire `auth.oidc` block — issuer, audience, jwks_uri, required_scope and the identity gate (allowed_subjects / allowed_usernames / required_role) — is read by nobody and discarded with no error and no log. That is a larger silent no-op than any of the four options the function does police, and it is security policy.
failure: `parseConfig({identity:{handle:'a'}, topics:['ctx'], auth:{mode:'builtin', oidc:{issuer:'https://kc.example/realms/p', required_role:'parley-owner'}}})` parses cleanly (AuthSchema's superRefine returns early unless mode === 'oidc') and `createRemoteAuthApp(plugin, cfg, {publicUrl, verifyOwner})` resolves the built-in OAuth AS. Reproduced: parsed auth = `{"mode":"builtin","oidc":{...,"required_role":"parley-owner","clock_skew_s":30}}`, booted = built-in OAuth AS. An operator who flips `mode` back to `builtin` while leaving the realm block in place gets a bridge with none of the gating they wrote and nothing at boot naming the cause — the mirror image of the case examples/self-host-remote/test/builtin-only-options.test.ts already guards for env vars.
remediation: Extend the mode/input consistency rule from `opts` to `cfg` in the same place: in `assertOptionsMatchMode` (or a sibling called beside it) throw when `cfg.auth.mode !== 'oidc'` and `cfg.auth.oidc !== undefined`, naming the block and telling the operator to remove it or switch modes. Mirror it in AuthSchema's superRefine so the schema and the factory agree.
testUpgrade: The CLASS is 'an input the selected auth mode never reads is accepted rather than refused'. Generalise the existing MODE_OPTIONS table in invariants.test.ts (which today is derived from remote-auth.ts's MODE_ONLY_OPTIONS source text and covers only `opts`) into a table over BOTH containers: rows of {source: 'opts'|'cfg.auth', key, mode-that-uses-it}, each asserting the factory throws naming the key under the other mode. Deriving the cfg rows from AuthSchema's shape means a future `auth.builtin` block is covered the day it lands.

summary: `freePort()` is byte-identical across six files in this one directory (keycloak.e2e, oidc-remote, error-surface, remote, invariants, teardown), `baseCfg()` is byte-identical across four (oidc-remote, error-surface, invariants, teardown), and `fakeRes()` is restated in two (oauth-provider, crypto-wiring). The package already has `src/testing/` as its shared-fixture home — fake-oidc.ts, fake-plugin.ts, tool-harness.ts, regex-corpus.ts all live there — so this is duplication with the destination already built and used by these same files.
failure: Not a runtime failure: a maintenance one. Changing the port-allocation strategy (e.g. binding to a specific interface, or retrying on a race between `s.close()` and the caller's `listen`) requires six identical edits in one directory, and any file that gets missed drifts silently because each copy is only exercised by its own suite. Verified by md5 of the 10-line body: invariants.test.ts and teardown.test.ts hash identically, and the other four differ only in trailing context.
remediation: Move `freePort` and `baseCfg` into `src/testing/` (e.g. `src/testing/net.ts` and the existing config helpers) and import them in all six files; collapse the two `fakeRes` copies into one exported builder with the query/body overrides both call sites need. No behavioural test changes — these are fixtures, not assertions.
testUpgrade: The CLASS is 'a fixture restated per test file inside one package'. Add a package-scoped hygiene row beside the existing scanners in hygiene.test.ts: hash the body of every top-level `function <name>(` / `const <name> = ` declaration across `src/**/*.test.ts` and fail on any body hash appearing in more than one file, with an allowlist that must name a reason. That is location-independent, catches the next copied helper rather than these three, and lives next to the guards that already scan this directory.

summary: `hardenErrorSurface` installs one terminal handler for the whole app and answers every uncaught error as `text/plain`. That is right for the browser-facing OAuth routes, but `/mcp` is a JSON-RPC endpoint whose own failure path (transport/http.ts handlePost's catch) answers with a JSON-RPC error object. The same endpoint therefore returns two incompatible media types depending on which layer failed, and a conformant MCP client that parses the body gets a JSON syntax error instead of a structured one.
failure: POST /mcp with a valid bearer and a body over express.json()'s 100 KB limit -> `413` with body `413 Payload Too Large` as `text/plain`. POST /mcp with a body that makes the handler throw -> `500` with `{"jsonrpc":"2.0","error":{"code":-32603,...}}` as `application/json`. error-surface.test.ts's own FRONT_DOORS table encodes the first case (`terminal: { route: '/mcp', trigger: 'body over the 100 KB parser limit (json)', status: 413 }`) and asserts the text form, so the divergence is pinned rather than noticed.
remediation: Make the terminal handler content-negotiate on the route it is terminating: keep the text/plain body for the browser front-door paths, and emit the same JSON-RPC error envelope handlePost uses when the failing request targets `mcpPath`. Pass `mcpPath` into `hardenErrorSurface` (both factories already know it) rather than sniffing `req.path`, so it cannot drift from the route actually registered.
testUpgrade: The CLASS is 'two layers of one endpoint answer the same class of failure in different media types'. Parameterize the existing error-surface matrix by FAILING LAYER as well as by front door: for each route, drive {parser-level failure, handler-level failure, no-route-matched} and assert the response's content-type and body shape are the SAME for all three on that route — and that no body contains a filesystem path. That row shape also catches the next middleware added in front of /mcp.

summary: filterReachable budgets only the peer-pattern direction. The opposite direction — the caller's own screened `post_topics` regexes run against peer-ADVERTISED topics via `canPostTo` — is unbounded in count and unbudgeted in time, so one page of legal presence beats freezes the single-threaded bridge for a minute.
failure: Post 128 presence beats to `parley-presence`, each self-declaring a distinct `handle` and 64 distinct 64-character `topics` (every value inside MAX_RECORD_TOPICS / MAX_TOPIC_LEN / MAX_HANDLE_LEN — one writer, one credential, no spoofing needed since `handle` is self-reported). Operator config carries 16 `post_topics` sources that `isRedosSafeSource` ACCEPTS (e.g. `a?`x16 + `a`x16 + `b`, ~0.4 ms per 64-char non-match). One `parley_list_users` call then runs 128 x 64 = 8192 topics through `Allowlist.has`, i.e. 131k screened matches. Measured in-repo: filterReachable took 53,806 ms of synchronous CPU. With a SINGLE such pattern it is still 3.2 s. Node is single-threaded, so every in-flight long-poll, every heartbeat and every other HTTP request stalls for that whole window, and the call is repeatable. Worse, `peerReach()`'s PEER_PATTERN_BUDGET_MS deadline is armed at the top of filterReachable and is entirely consumed by this loop, so `reaches()` afterwards always returns false — the budgeted direction is silently switched off and legitimate peers vanish from the roster.
remediation: Make the deadline whole-call and check it on BOTH directions. Hoist the `Date.now() + PEER_PATTERN_BUDGET_MS` deadline into `filterReachable` itself, check it before each `canPostTo(t)` as well as before each `reaches(...)`, and stop matching (dropping reach, not safety) once it is spent. Additionally cap the topics per entry that are put through `canPostTo` — an entry's `topics` array is attacker-sized up to MAX_RECORD_TOPICS and `Allowlist.has` is the caller's regex bank. `regex-safety.ts` already states the contract being broken here: the ambiguity bound is PER SOURCE and 'a caller that matches one input against a collection of screened sources ... must also bound HOW MANY it holds' — this call site bounds neither the sources nor the inputs.
testUpgrade: Guard the CLASS 'a tool call multiplies untrusted count x config count and only one factor is budgeted'. In presence.test.ts's `untrusted presence history cannot exceed a CPU or byte budget` table, replace the `canPostTo: () => false` stub with a REAL `new Allowlist(myTopics, { postPatterns }).has`, built from the same `worstAcceptedSource()` corpus already computed for peer patterns, and add two dimensions to the table: record `topics` count (1 vs MAX_RECORD_TOPICS) and caller `post_topics` count (0 vs MAX_POST_TOPICS). Assert the WHOLE-CALL wall clock of `filterReachable` stays under CPU_BUDGET_MS in every cell, and add a row asserting that a hostile page does not starve the peer-pattern direction (a benign peer whose postTopics match one of my topics must still be returned). The existing table is too narrow in exactly three ways at once: stubbed predicate, one topic per record, and no caller patterns.

summary: The suite's dedicated CPU-budget table for hostile presence history passes `canPostTo: () => false` and gives each record a single topic, so it structurally cannot observe the dominant cost term in `filterReachable`. It counts as coverage for a bound it never measures.
failure: `untrusted presence history cannot exceed a CPU or byte budget` (presence.test.ts:562-657) crosses handles x instances x patterns x caller-topics and asserts `< CPU_BUDGET_MS` (500 ms). Every row passes `canPostTo: () => false` — a free function — and every hostile record advertises exactly one `topics` entry (`topics: [padded(...)]`). The real production wiring is `canPostTo: (t) => deps.allow.has(t)` (list-users-tool.ts:123), which compiles and runs up to MAX_POST_TOPICS operator regexes per topic. So the one cell that costs 53.8 s in production is the one cell the table cannot express, and it stays green. The neighbouring row at presence.test.ts:464 has the same stub.
remediation: Never let a cost-budget test stub the predicate whose cost is being budgeted. Construct the real collaborator (an `Allowlist` with a worst-accepted `post_topics` corpus) and make its size a table dimension; where a collaborator genuinely must be faked, assert its invocation COUNT as well as the wall clock, so a stub that answers instantly still pins the multiplication factor.

summary: `resumeAfter` guards a `since` cursor against the wrong STORE but not against the wrong TOPIC: the rowid is store-global, so a cursor minted for topic A is honoured verbatim when replayed against topic B and silently skips B's history below that rowid.
failure: post 'b0' to topic b (rowid 1), five rows to topic a (rowids 2..6), 'b1' to topic b (rowid 7). `fetchRecent({topic:'a'})` -> nextCursor `<storeId>.6`. The README's own reasoning ("absorbing it would ... wedge that topic's catch-up silently") is why the store-id prefix exists; the same silent-skip hazard survives one level down.
remediation: Either bind the topic into the cursor the way the store id is bound (`<storeId>.<topicHash>.<rowid>`, rejecting/replaying on mismatch), or document explicitly in README and in the `resumeAfter` contract that a cursor is only meaningful for the topic that minted it and that a cross-topic `since` skips history. summary: The README tells the operator both that clearing core's persisted read-state after a store reset is "no longer load-bearing" and, 30 lines later, that they must "discard core's persisted read-state *and* restart the bridge" — and the reason given for the second (core's in-memory seen-set) does not support discarding read-state at all.

summary: `restrictMode` unconditionally narrows any store with group/other bits to 0600 with no opt-out, so a deliberately group-shared store (the multi-UID topology the README itself acknowledges) is silently converted into one only the first bridge's UID can open.

summary: `subscriptionHealth()` is a public plugin API that exists in exactly one backend and, by the README's own admission, has no route to any user of the shipped product — either the seam is missing a liveness capability all ten backends need, or this is code plus ~700 lines of tests serving a hypothetical embedder.

summary: `labelled()` decides "this error is already mine" by testing `err.message.startsWith('parley-redis:')` — a marker the SERVER can spell. summary: The read loop's `try { handler(...) } catch { /* handler is best-effort; never break the loop (DESIGN §6) */ }` is graded by nothing — not in this package, not in `packages/conformance` (no case anywhere passes a throwing handler; `grep throw packages/conformance/src/cases/*` finds only test-internal throws). summary: `assertStorable` claims to refuse every seam argument "PostgreSQL's TEXT type cannot hold" but only tests for U+0000; an unpaired surrogate is equally unrepresentable in UTF-8 and is silently transcoded to U+FFFD by the driver, so two distinct topics collapse into one shared history and content is silently altered.

The returned `Message.topic` is `room-�`, not the topic asked for, and the content comes back as `lone � surrogate`. Derive the rule from "can this string be encoded to UTF-8 losslessly" (e.g. compare `Buffer.from(v,'utf8').toString('utf8')` to `v`) rather than from a hand-listed character, so the next unrepresentable shape is covered too.

summary: The `pg` fake cannot transcode, so the two lone-surrogate CORPUS rows are graded only on "was not refused" and "a query was issued" — which is true while the real server silently mangles the value; the file's own comment says these values "must keep working", and against a real server they do not.
