summary: A `subscribe(topic, B)` that joins an in-flight first subscribe appends its handler only after `startSubscription` resolves, but the first drain may already have delivered — and advanced `sub.lastSeen` past — messages that landed while B's call was in flight, so B's successfully-resolved subscribe silently starts behind the tail.
failure: Traced, not reproduced. `subscribe(t, A)` is in flight; `subscribe(t, B)` takes the `this.subscribing.get(channel)` branch and awaits. `startSubscription` sets `lastSeen = MAX(seq)`, LISTENs, registers, and calls `drain(sub)`. A NOTIFY for a row posted after B called `subscribe` drains and fans out to `sub.handlers` — which is `[A]` — and sets `sub.lastSeen` past it. Only then does `(await inFlight).handlers.push(B)` run. B's `subscribe` resolves successfully having missed a message posted after it was called, contradicting the method's own JSDoc: "both the tail and the LISTEN are established BEFORE this resolves, so nothing posted afterwards can fall between them." Push loss is recovered by catch-up only if core is also running the cursor path for that topic.
remediation: Either register the joining handler before the drain can advance `lastSeen` (append to `sub.handlers` synchronously when the in-flight entry is created, holding the handler list rather than the promise), or narrow the JSDoc to state the guarantee only for the subscriber that establishes the subscription. Fail-fast is also acceptable: reject a concurrent join rather than resolve it with a weaker guarantee.
testUpgrade: Parameterize `subscribe-race.test.ts` over (first-subscriber, joiner-via-inFlight, joiner-via-live-fast-path) × (message posted before / during / after the first drain), asserting for each arm exactly which handlers must see the message and that the arm is the DECLARED one — so a change to when a joiner is armed fails rather than quietly changing the contract for one arm.

summary: `boundedLocalpart`'s over-long branch bypasses `safeName`'s disjointness guarantee, so an over-long topic and a crafted short topic fold to the SAME room alias. Its own JSDoc claims "the fold stays injective"; it is not. Two topics sharing one room is a total topic-isolation bypass in per-topic (production) mode, where `belongs()` returns true for every `m.room.message` in the room.
failure: Reproduced in the worktree (`boundedLocalpart` at server_name `parley.local`): topic A = 'x'.repeat(400) -> localpart `parley_` + 'x'*222 + `-ad8eb84320`. Feed the localpart's tail back as topic B = 'x'*222 + '-ad8eb84320' (234 chars, naturally alias-safe, length exactly at the budget so it passes through `safeName` unchanged because `isDisambiguated` only recognises a 16-hex suffix). boundedLocalpart(B) === boundedLocalpart(A), byte for byte. Both topics resolve `#parley_xxx…-ad8eb84320:parley.local`, so a `post` to B lands in A's room and `subscribe`/`fetchRecent` on A deliver B's traffic into the agent session (and vice versa). No brute force and no hash collision is required — the collision is deterministic and constructible from A's alias alone. A `post_topics` regex broad enough to admit a model-chosen topic makes it model-reachable.
remediation: Make the truncated form shape-disjoint from the pass-through form rather than probabilistically distinct: e.g. mint truncated names under a reserved prefix the untruncated branch can never produce (`parleyh_…` vs `parley_…`), or extend `isDisambiguated`/`safeName` to recognise the truncated shape so a raw topic matching it is itself disambiguated. Either way the truncated branch must not be constructible as a `safeName` fixed point.
testUpgrade: Guard the CLASS 'the fold is injective across ALL of its branches', not the one pair. Replace the two hand-picked pairs (`a/b`/`a_b`, `<base>-one`/`<base>-two` in room-isolation.fake.test.ts:227,282) with a generator: build a topic corpus that includes, for every seed topic, (a) the seed, (b) `boundedLocalpart(seed, server).slice('parley_'.length)` re-fed as a topic, (c) `safeName(seed, sanitizeAlias)` re-fed as a topic, sweeping seed lengths across the budget boundary (budget-1, budget, budget+1, 4x budget) and both ASCII and multi-byte alphabets; assert `new Set(topics.map(boundedLocalpart)).size === topics.length`. Also sweep `server_name` lengths, since the budget (and thus `keep`) moves with it.

summary: The plugin adopts whatever room a guessable, deterministic alias resolves to, with no check of who created it, its join rule, or its membership — while the README claims topic rooms are invite-only and that an uninvited account "cannot post messages that core would deliver into a live Claude Code session as `<channel>` events". That claim holds only for rooms this plugin created.
failure: Trace: `resolveOrCreateRoom` (session.ts:174) calls `lookupAlias` FIRST and, on a hit, `joinRoom` + return — `createRoom`/`preset` is never reached. `existingRoom` (session.ts:138-147) does the same on every read path. `joinRoom` throws only on 403. Synapse's default `alias_creation_rules` lets any local account create any alias, so an unprivileged account (or, under federation, a remote one) pre-creates `#parley_ctx-payments:parley.local` as a `public_chat` room before the bridge first posts. The bridge then: resolves it, joins (200), `post`s the agent's output into the attacker's room (exfiltration), and `subscribe` delivers every attacker message through `deliver()` -> core -> `<channel>` events into the live Claude Code session (the prompt-injection surface DESIGN §14 exists to minimise). Nothing is logged; the operator sees a working bridge. `packages/bridge-matrix/test/provisioning.fake.test.ts` grades `aliasExists: true` only for 'no createRoom happened' — the adopted room's provenance is graded nowhere.
remediation: Verify a room this account did not create before using it: `GET /rooms/<id>/state/m.room.create` and compare `sender` (and optionally `m.room.join_rules`) against `this.userId` plus a configurable `expect_creators` allowlist; refuse or, at minimum, emit a `[parley-matrix] SECURITY:` stderr line through `configRisks`-style reporting naming the alias, the foreign creator and the join rule. Correct the README's security section to scope the invite-only guarantee to rooms this plugin provisioned, and note that an adopted alias is trust-on-first-use.
testUpgrade: Guard the CLASS 'a resource the plugin ADOPTS is held to the same trust bar as one it PROVISIONS'. Add a `FakeSynapse` knob for a pre-existing room with a chosen `m.room.create` sender and `join_rule`, then a table over {creator: self | foreign} x {join_rule: invite | public} x every ENTRY_POINT (post / fetchRecent / subscribe), asserting the declared outcome (reject, or warn with a line naming alias+creator+join rule) for each. Extend the existing `SIDE_EFFECTS` table so an adopt path that issues no provenance GET fails there too, and mirror it in the live provisioning case that today only reads back a room the run itself created.

summary: The over-long branch mints a `MIN_HASH_LEN` (10 hex = 40-bit) disambiguator, re-introducing exactly the width core rejected — and core's rejection names this exact fold.
failure: `boundedLocalpart` uses `createHash('sha1')…slice(0, MIN_HASH_LEN)` (10 hex chars) while every other topic on this backend gets `safeName`'s `DEFAULT_HASH_LEN` = 16. `packages/bridge-core/src/topic-name.ts:29` states: "That is why 40 bits was not enough: over the Matrix alias fold, which rejects everything outside `[A-Za-z0-9._-]`, three lossy positions in a victim topic already put a collision in reach, and a collision routes one topic's traffic into another's backend channel." So for any topic past the 255-byte alias bound, bridge-matrix ships the width core documented as insufficient for bridge-matrix. Input: any topic longer than `248 - len(server_name) - 7` bytes -> a room alias whose only disambiguator is 40 bits over a fold with a small illegal alphabet.
remediation: Use `DEFAULT_HASH_LEN` in the truncation branch (widen `keep` accordingly, and raise the `keep < 1` guard's threshold to match), or import the width from core rather than restating a floor as a default. `MIN_HASH_LEN` is documented as 'a caller may ask for this narrow a suffix deliberately; nothing mints it by default' — this mints it by default.
testUpgrade: Guard the CLASS 'no shipped backend mints a disambiguator narrower than DEFAULT_HASH_LEN'. Parameterize over every fold a backend exports (`sanitizeAlias`, the NATS/XMPP/postgres equivalents) x topic lengths straddling each backend's own name bound, asserting the minted suffix length equals `DEFAULT_HASH_LEN`; and pin it structurally by importing `DEFAULT_HASH_LEN` rather than the literal 16, so a core change moves both sides together. `packages/bridge-core/src/stated-bounds.test.ts` grades safeName's own widths but never the per-backend truncation branches that bypass it.

summary: The README states the topic->room alias twice as `#parley_<sanitizedTopic>:<server_name>` and never mentions the disambiguating hash suffix or the 255-byte truncation, so an operator computing a room's alias by hand gets the wrong one for any topic that is not already alias-legal.
failure: README lines 15 and 86 both give `#parley_<sanitizedTopic>:<server_name>`. The code (alias.ts via core's `safeName`) actually produces `#parley_ops_prod-1608f4e357676264:fake` for topic `ops:prod` and `#parley_team_frontend-222ee3741b0781e7:fake` for `team/frontend` (both pinned as literals in room-isolation.fake.test.ts:199-200), and a truncated `…-<10hex>` form past 255 bytes. `sanitizedTopic` is also never defined (which characters fold to `_`). The README's own operational advice depends on getting this right: 'leave the rooms of retired topics out of band (any Matrix client, or `POST /rooms/<id>/leave`)' (line 54) and the multi-session `invite` guidance both require the operator to identify the room by alias.
remediation: State the real fold in the seam-mapping row and the security section: characters outside `[A-Za-z0-9._-]` fold to `_`, and any topic whose fold is lossy (or whose alias would exceed 255 bytes) carries a `-<hex>` disambiguating suffix over the raw topic, so distinct topics can never share a room. Give one worked example.
testUpgrade: Guard the CLASS 'a name-mapping formula stated in a README is the one the code computes', not this sentence. Extend `shipped-artifacts.test.ts`'s doc-parity block (which already grades cursor SHAPES against README + DESIGN) with a fold table: for a set of topics covering {already-legal, lossy, over-long}, assert the README contains the localpart the plugin's own `boundedLocalpart` produces — driven off the same `FOLDS` table `room-isolation.fake.test.ts` uses, so one table feeds both the wire assertion and the doc assertion and a new fold branch cannot be added doc-silently.

summary: `disconnect()` called while `connect()` is still awaiting `xmpp.start()` observes `this.xmpp === undefined`, so it stops nothing; `connect()` then completes and assigns `this.xmpp = xmpp` on a plugin whose `stopped` is already true. The plugin ends up holding a live, never-stopped `@xmpp/client` while refusing every seam call — exactly the orphan the two dedicated lifecycle suites declare they forbid.
failure: Reproduced with a FakeXmpp whose `start()` is gated: `const c = plugin.connect(cfg); await plugin.disconnect(); release(); await c;` → observed `stops=0, held=true, stopped=true`. The abandoned-but-held client is never stopped, so `@xmpp/reconnect` keeps redialling and re-presenting `backend_config.password` and holds the event loop open (the process never exits after shutdown); meanwhile every `post`/`fetchRecent`/`subscribe` throws 'not connected' and a retrying supervisor's next `connect()` throws 'already connected — call disconnect() before connect() again', so the instance is wedged until someone calls `disconnect()` a second time.
remediation: Take ownership of the client before awaiting `start()`, or re-check the teardown flag after it: set a connect-generation/`connecting` token at the top of `connect()`, and after `await xmpp.start()` resolves do `if (this.stopped || generation !== this.generation) { await xmpp.stop().catch(() => undefined); throw new Error('disconnected during connect'); }` before assigning `this.xmpp`. Symmetrically, make `disconnect()` await/cancel an in-flight connect rather than assuming `this.xmpp` is the whole of the transport state.
testUpgrade: lifecycle-order.test.ts's table is sequential-only — every row awaits each call before the next, so no row can express a race, and its own stated invariant ('exactly one client is live afterwards, and it is the one the plugin holds') is unreachable for concurrent orderings. Widen the generator from a list of sequences to a list of INTERLEAVINGS: parameterize FakeXmpp with a gate on each of `start()`/`stop()`, and for each pair of lifecycle calls (connect|disconnect|connect-after-connect) run both orders with the first call suspended at each gate point, asserting the same invariant already asserted per row — `fakes.filter(f => f.stops === 0)` equals exactly `[the held client]` (or `[]`), plus `stopped === (held === undefined)`. That class covers connect/disconnect, disconnect/disconnect and connect/connect races, not just this instance.

summary: The occupancy-loss give-up counter measures the interval between consecutive LOSSES (`now - prior.at`, where `at` is the previous loss), not how long occupancy was actually HELD. A room whose occupancy ends rarely but regularly — well inside a minute apart, but with the connection healthy 99% of the time in between — burns through the 6-loss budget and has its live push permanently abandoned.
failure: Reproduced with fake timers: a room that ends occupancy once and then stays healthy for 55 s, repeated. Observed `joined=true` after losses 1-6 and `joined=false` from loss 7 onward, with the log line '7 consecutive times, each within 60000 ms of the previous — not re-entering it again'. So after ~6.5 minutes of ~99.6% healthy occupancy, live push for that topic is dead until an unrelated `post`/`fetch_recent` happens to re-enter the room — while the ladder was designed to stop a room that ends occupancy 'as fast as the connection can send presence' (~13 s for 6 losses).
remediation: Record the time occupancy was last successfully (re-)established — e.g. stamp `rejoins[room].heldSince` when `ensureJoinedRoom` resolves — and reset `losses` to 1 when `now - heldSince >= REJOIN_WINDOW_MS`. That is what the constant's own JSDoc already claims ('Occupancy held this long counts as recovered'), and it keeps the ladder's real purpose (bounding a hot re-join loop) while never abandoning a room that is merely flaky.
testUpgrade: rejoin-ladder.test.ts drives only the hot case (`kickOnJoin`, losses back-to-back) and so is satisfied by either predicate. Parameterize it over the HOLD DURATION between losses — a table of e.g. [0 ms, 1 s, 30 s, 55 s, 61 s, 5 min] × 8 losses — asserting one property per row: the plugin gives up only when the room never held occupancy for `REJOIN_WINDOW_MS`, and re-enters indefinitely otherwise. That generator also catches the mirror-image bug (a counter that resets so eagerly the storm cap stops firing), which the current single-shape case cannot.

summary: `REJOIN_WINDOW_MS`'s JSDoc reads 'Occupancy held this long counts as recovered: the consecutive-loss count starts over', but the code never measures how long occupancy was held — it compares the current loss's timestamp against the PREVIOUS LOSS's. A reader tuning the constant, or auditing whether the give-up is safe, is told a recovery rule the plugin does not implement.
failure: Read the claim, then the only site that uses the constant (rooms.ts:71): `const losses = prior !== undefined && now - prior.at < REJOIN_WINDOW_MS ? prior.losses + 1 : 1;` where `prior.at` is set at the previous `onOccupancyLost`. Nothing anywhere records a join time, so 'occupancy held this long' is not a quantity the plugin computes. A room that held occupancy for 55 s between every loss is counted as never having recovered — see the reproduction in the finding above.
remediation: Either implement the documented predicate (track `heldSince` at successful join and compare against it), which is the better behaviour, or restate the JSDoc to the predicate the code measures — 'two losses closer together than this are consecutive' — matching the give-up log line and the README, which both already say 'within a minute of the previous'.
testUpgrade: The README sentence is already parsed back out and pinned by rejoin-ladder.test.ts's second describe. Extend that class from the README to the SOURCE claim: assert the log line's predicate wording and the constant's JSDoc describe the same quantity the code branches on — most durably by exporting the predicate as a named pure function (`isConsecutiveLoss(prior, now)` / `hasRecovered(heldSince, now)`) and unit-testing it directly, so the doc sentence and the branch cannot drift apart in the first place.

summary: When `connect()` replaces a live connection while `subscribe()` is parked in its `POST /api/v1/register` round-trip, the abandonment path resolves `conn.rest` AFTER the await, so the DELETE for the queue minted on the OLD server is issued against the NEW server with the NEW server's credentials. The old server's queue is never released, and a foreign queue id is disclosed to a possibly different host.
failure: Probe (reproduced): two fakes A and B; `A.holdResponse('POST /api/v1/register', 800)`; `plugin.subscribe(topic, …)` (not awaited); after 200ms `plugin.connect({site_url: B.url})`. Result: `A registers 1, A deletes 0` and `B registers 0, B deletes 1`. Server A keeps an orphan event queue for its full ~10-minute GC window against the bot's queue budget, and B receives `DELETE /api/v1/events?queue_id=fq-1` for an id it never minted. This directly falsifies README line 16 ("its queues are deleted against the site it was made with") and the `zulip releases every event queue it opens` ledger claim. The same shape sits at `wake.ts` `armDedicatedQueue`'s `release` → `conn.deleteQueueDetached(reg.queue_id)`, which after a reconnect issues a second, spurious DELETE against the new server.
remediation: Capture the transport (and the generation) at the point the resource is created and use that captured handle for its release: e.g. `const rest = conn.rest; … if (!alive()) { await rest.deleteQueue(reg.queue_id); return; }`, and have `deleteQueueDetached` take the `ZulipHttp` that minted the queue rather than reading `this.rest`. Alternatively register the queue in `conn.queues` before the liveness check so `close()` owns its release — but only if `close()` is guaranteed to run after registration, which it is not here, so the captured-handle fix is the durable one.
testUpgrade: CLASS: every server-side resource is released against the connection that minted it, on every path, including paths that are mid-handshake when the connection is replaced. Extend `subscription-lifecycle.test.ts`'s `PARK_POINTS` with handshake-internal points (`held POST /api/v1/register`, `held GET /api/v1/messages` during the tail probe) and cross them with `CONNECTION_ENDINGS` filtered to `reconnects`, against BOTH `TARGETS` (same server / different server). Assert per-server ledgers: `old.requestCount('DELETE /api/v1/events') >= old.requestCount('POST /api/v1/register')` AND `new.requestCount('DELETE /api/v1/events') === 0` before the new connection does any work. The existing `zulip releases every event queue it opens` table is too narrow — it only counts totals on one fake and only after the handshake has completed.

summary: `subscribe()` resolves successfully when the connection it addressed was torn down or replaced during its handshake — `if (!alive()) { …; return; }` returns normally. `post`, `fetchRecent` and `resolveIdentity` all throw `Zulip connection was replaced…` for the identical race. Core's `startPushLoop` treats a resolved `subscribe` as a live subscription and never retries, so live push for that topic is permanently and silently dead.
failure: Probe (reproduced): `subscribe(topic, handler)` parked in a held `POST /api/v1/register`, then `connect({site_url: other})` lands. `subscribe outcome: resolved`. `packages/bridge-core/src/transport/push-loop.ts:68` awaits `plugin.subscribe(topic, handler)` once per allowlisted topic and only branches on a rejection; a resolve means core records the topic as subscribed. No `<channel>` event will ever be emitted for it, and nothing is written to stderr. The same silent resolve occurs for a plain `disconnect()` racing the handshake.
remediation: Replace the bare `return` with `conn.assertGeneration(generation)` (or an equivalent throw naming the replaced connection), so `subscribe` fails the same way every other seam call does — after best-effort releasing the queue against the transport that minted it (see the sibling finding). Fail-fast is the house rule; a resolved promise that started nothing is the no-op `CLAUDE.md` forbids.
testUpgrade: CLASS: no seam call answers — or claims success — from a connection it did not address. Add `subscribe` as a row to `subscription-lifecycle.test.ts`'s `SEAM_CALLS` table (routes `POST /api/v1/register` and `GET /api/v1/messages`, since the handshake makes both), so it is graded by the same `rejects.toThrow(/connection was replaced/i)` assertion the other four already carry, crossed with `ENTRIES` × `TARGETS`. Today the table enumerates exactly the calls that already behave correctly, which is why the one that does not was invisible.

summary: `readWindow` computes `deadlineMs = budgetedDeadlineMs(opts.deadline)` ONCE, outside the pagination loop, and hands the same value to every page. `fetchWithRetry` measures its wall-clock budget from its own start, so page N gets the caller's ORIGINAL budget again rather than what is left. `ZulipPlugin.fetchRecent`'s JSDoc states the opposite: "`blockMs` is a ceiling on the WHOLE call… every request the call makes carries the budget that is left, so none of them can spend it on a rate-limit hint."
failure: Probe (reproduced) against the in-process fake: 5101 messages on a topic, `holdResponse('GET /api/v1/messages', 800)`, then `fetchRecent({topic, since, limit: 6000, blockMs: 500})` → 2 pages, elapsed 1655ms (3.3× the stated ceiling). With `blockMs: 2000` / hold 1200ms → 2428ms. The rate-limit half is the sharper harm: page 2 is offered `deadlineMs = (budget at page 1's start) + 500`, so a `Retry-After` hint that the caller's budget has already been exhausted by is accepted and waited out — exactly the hazard the comment on `budgetedDeadlineMs` says it prevents. Not reachable through core today (`MAX_FETCH_LIMIT = 1000` < `MAX_MESSAGES_PER_FETCH = 5000`, and the catch-up path passes no `blockMs`), but the plugin is a published package whose seam contract is what a direct caller reads.
remediation: Move the `budgetedDeadlineMs(opts.deadline)` call inside the `while (remaining > 0)` loop so each page carries what is actually left, and break out of the loop when the remaining budget is non-positive rather than issuing a page that cannot be answered in time.
testUpgrade: CLASS: a per-call budget is recomputed at every request the call makes, not once at entry. Widen `blocking-fetch.test.ts`'s `zulip blocking fetchRecent never overruns its blockMs` table with a `limit` dimension crossing single-page and multi-page reads (`[100, MAX_MESSAGES_PER_FETCH + 1]`), seeding enough history for the multi-page row, and keep the `elapsed <= blockMs + SLACK_MS` bound on both. Add a row whose 429 hint is armed on the SECOND history read via `setResponseHook`, so a hint accepted on a later page fails the bound. Today every row in that table uses the default `limit: 100`, i.e. exactly one page, so no row can see a per-page budget.

summary: `close()` does `await Promise.race([Promise.allSettled(exits), delay(TEARDOWN_TIMEOUT_MS)])` and never clears the `delay` timer. `delay` is `new Promise(r => setTimeout(r, ms))` with no `unref`, so every `disconnect()` — including one where the loops exit immediately, which is the normal case — leaves a live 2000ms handle holding the Node event loop open.
failure: A library consumer that calls `await plugin.disconnect()` and then lets `main()` return sees the process linger ~2s past teardown with nothing left to do. `src/cli.ts` masks it because `shutdown()` ends in `process.exit(0)`, so no test observes it; the `zulip disconnect completes in bounded time` table asserts the promise settles, not that the process can exit. Same effect on every test run: `useZulip`'s `afterEach` disconnects, leaving a pending timer per case.
remediation: Use a cancellable timeout for the race — e.g. keep a `setTimeout` handle and `clearTimeout` it in a `finally`, or race against `conn.timedWait(TEARDOWN_TIMEOUT_MS).waited` and call its `release()` afterwards, since `timedWait` already clears its own timer and deregisters itself.
testUpgrade: CLASS: teardown leaves no live handle behind. Add a case that, after `plugin.disconnect()` resolves, asserts the package holds no pending timers — e.g. compare `process.getActiveResourcesInfo()` (or a `vi.useFakeTimers()` `vi.getTimerCount()`) before subscribe and after disconnect, parameterized over `CONNECTION_ENDINGS` and over 0/1/3 live subscriptions so a handle leaked by any teardown path fails. This grades the invariant (no surviving handle) rather than any one timer, so it survives a rewrite of the race.

summary: The fake models `consume()`'s `status()` as an immediately-completing empty async generator, so `await statusTask` in the live loop is unconditionally instantaneous in every fake-backed test. The drain-on-stale invariant the live loop depends on is therefore graded nowhere: mutating `live.ts:82` `if (stale) continue;` to `break;` leaves the entire 1537-test suite green, while the same change hangs the loop forever against a real JetStream server.
failure: Applied the mutation `live.ts:82 continue -> break` and ran `PARLEY_NATS_SERVERS=127.0.0.1:14222 npx vitest run packages/bridge-nats`: `Test Files 23 passed (23) / Tests 1537 passed (1537)`. A separate probe against `nats:2.10-alpine -js` running the same shape (ephemeral AckPolicy.None consumer, `consume()`, a `closeOnConsumerLoss`-equivalent status task, `void iter.close()` then exit the message loop) printed `drain -> settled` and `break -> HUNG` (status task still pending after 5s). Production consequence of the undetected shape: a break in `m.info.deliverySequence` on a HEALTHY link (the reconnect-then-gap case `outage.test.ts` names) parks the live loop at `live.ts:104 await statusTask` forever — `subscribe` goes permanently deaf, silently, until the process restarts. The one live test that reaches the stale path ('delivers a message the server pushed into a link that was already gone') does so with the socket reset, where the real status iterator also terminates, so it cannot discriminate.
remediation: Make the fake's `consume()` iterator expose a status source with the same lifecycle as nats.js: a live async queue that ends only when the iterator's teardown actually runs (i.e. after the message loop is drained), never a pre-completed generator. Add the close-then-drain vs close-then-break semantic to `jetstream-agreement.ts` so it is asserted against a real server as well as the fake.
testUpgrade: Guard the CLASS 'a consumer-iterator lifecycle semantic the fake short-circuits'. Add a parameterized agreement row `exitMode: 'drain' | 'break'` x `link: 'alive' | 'dropped'` whose `expected` is 'the status watcher settles within N ms', run from BOTH `window.test.ts` (fake) and `jetstream-agreement-live.test.ts` (real server) off the same literal — that construction is what makes a divergence red instead of a suite-wide false green. Separately widen `subscribe-loop.test.ts` with a LIVE row that induces a delivery-sequence gap without dropping the socket (delete and re-add the ephemeral consumer under the same name at a higher `opt_start_seq`, or consume the same consumer from a second connection) and assert the handler resumes; today every delivery-hole row is fake-only.

summary: The 'has an agreement row for every primitive the fake models' assertion derives `jsm.*` and `js.*` primitives from the fake's own object keys, but hardcodes the consumer-iterator surface as `['fetch','consume']`. Any semantic modelled on the iterator returned by `consume()`/`fetch()` — `status()`, `close()` — is exempt from the completeness gate by construction, which is exactly the hole that let the previous finding exist.
failure: `fakePrimitives()` builds its list from `Object.keys(jsm.streams)`, `Object.keys(jsm.consumers)`, `Object.keys(js.consumers)`, `Object.keys(js)` and then the literal `['fetch','consume'].map(k => 'consumer.'+k)`. The fake's `consume()` result object exposes `status` and `close` (fake-jetstream.ts:302-305); neither appears in `fakePrimitives()`, so `window.test.ts`'s `expect(fakePrimitives()).toEqual([...PRIMITIVES].sort())` passes with `status` modelled and unverified. Adding another iterator method to the fake would likewise arrive unpoliced, defeating the stated 'a primitive added to the fake with no agreement row fails here by default' property.
remediation: Derive the iterator surface too: instantiate the fake's `consume()` and `fetch()` results and enumerate their own keys into the primitive list (e.g. `consumer.consume.status`, `consumer.consume.close`), so PRIMITIVES must be extended and an agreement row written whenever the fake grows a method.
testUpgrade: Guard the CLASS 'a completeness lint whose enumeration is partly hand-written'. Replace the literal with a generator over `Object.keys(await (await js.consumers.get()).consume())` and `.fetch({max_messages:1})`, and add a self-test row that adds a dummy method to the fake's iterator and asserts the coverage assertion FAILS — a completeness check that has never been watched to fail is not a completeness check.

summary: The `retired() ||` half of the live loop's per-message guard is graded by nothing: removing it leaves the whole suite green. Either it prevents a message already queued in the iterator from reaching a handler after `disconnect()` has resolved — the property the class JSDoc explicitly claims — and that property is untested, or it is redundant and the JSDoc claim is unbacked.
failure: Mutated `live.ts:88` from `if (retired() || m.info.deliverySequence !== nextDelivery)` to `if (m.info.deliverySequence !== nextDelivery)` and ran the package suite: `Test Files 23 passed (23) / Tests 1537 passed (1537)`. `recovery.test.ts`'s 'stays dead when disconnect() lands Nms into the loop's cycle' rows cannot reach it — they publish only AFTER the reconnect, so the outer `while (running())` alone satisfies them; no case publishes into a live iterator and then tears down inside the delivery window.
remediation: Either add coverage that a handler is never invoked after `disconnect()` resolves with messages already queued in the iterator, or delete the `retired()` term and the JSDoc sentence that claims it. A guard whose removal is invisible is counted as coverage while defending nothing.
testUpgrade: Guard the CLASS 'a teardown guard inside a background loop that no case can fail'. Add a parameterized row over the teardown-interleaving axis already used by `lifecycle.test.ts` — {message queued in the iterator at teardown, message published during teardown, loop parked in backoff} x {fake, live} — recording the wall-clock of the last handler invocation and asserting it precedes the resolution of `disconnect()`. That form also catches a future guard moved or renamed, unlike an assertion on this exact expression.

summary: `validateRetentionDays` rejects 0, negatives and non-numbers at connect() but accepts any positive finite number. A value whose composed `max_age` exceeds int64 nanoseconds connects cleanly and then breaks every write with an opaque driver error naming neither the field nor the value — the exact failure mode `validatePrefix`, `assertKnownConfigKeys` and this function's own JSDoc exist to prevent.
failure: Against a real `nats:2.10-alpine -js`: `backend_config: { retention_days: 1e6 }` -> `connect()` resolves, then `post()` rejects with `NatsError: invalid json`. Same for `1e8` and `Number.MAX_SAFE_INTEGER`. `1e5` still works, so the real ceiling is ~106,751 days (int64 ns / 86_400_000_000_000, computed in `streams.ts:69`). An operator who writes `retention_days: 1000000` gets a bridge that starts, logs nothing, and fails every post and every subscribe with a message that mentions neither `retention_days` nor NATS retention.
remediation: In `validateRetentionDays`, also reject anything above the largest day count whose nanosecond conversion is both a safe integer and an int64 — derive the bound from `NS_PER_DAY` rather than a literal — with the same 'name the field, name the limit' error text the prefix validators use.
testUpgrade: Guard the CLASS 'a numeric config field validated only at its lower bound'. Extend config.test.ts's `retentions` table with rows generated from the ceiling constant (MAX_DAYS, MAX_DAYS + 1, MAX_DAYS * 10, Number.MAX_SAFE_INTEGER) asserting reject-at-connect naming the field for anything the server cannot carry and an exact `max_age` for the accepted ones; today the table's largest row is 30, so no row can reach the upper boundary. Apply the same generated-boundary shape to every numeric field this plugin accepts, so a field added later is bounded-by-default.

summary: The `conversations.history` walk encodes "pages arrive newest-first" as an unchecked property of a vendor-controlled body. Both the O(limit) retention trim (`collected.splice(0, collected.length - retain)`) and the no-`since` early exit (`if (collected.length >= limit) break`) are order-dependent, while every other field read out of an `ok:true` envelope in this package is validated with a named `SlackShapeError`. A page order the plugin does not expect produces silent, permanent history loss under a `nextCursor` that sits above it — precisely the failure `MAX_HISTORY_PAGES`' "THROW rather than break" comment says the walk must never produce.
failure: Reproduced: 500 seeded plain messages, pageSize 50, `fetchRecent({topic, since: asCursor('0'), limit: 1})` while the server pages OLDEST-first returns `['m299']` with `nextCursor = ts(m299)` instead of `['m0']` — m0..m298 are below the published cursor and no later catch-up revisits them. Same fixture, `fetchRecent({topic, limit: 3})` (no `since`) returns `['m47','m48','m49']` instead of the newest `['m497','m498','m499']`, so the default window and `parley_list_users` read the oldest end of the channel.
remediation: Make the retention and the walk termination order-independent rather than resting on the vendor. After pushing each page, `collected.sort((a,b) => compareTs(a.ts,b.ts))` and truncate the TAIL beyond `retain` (keeping the oldest) instead of `splice(0, …)`; drive the no-`since` break off the newest `limit` surfaced entries seen so far rather than off arrival position. Alternatively — and consistently with this package's own doctrine — validate the page: if a page is not descending by `ts`, throw a `SlackShapeError('conversations.history', 'returned a page that is not newest-first')` so the assumption is stated where it can fail loudly instead of losing history.
testUpgrade: Guard the CLASS "a walk decision that depends on a vendor-chosen ordering": give `FakeSlack` a page-order axis (`newest-first` | `oldest-first` | `shuffled`, seeded) and parameterize the existing `catchup-window.test.ts` drain tables and `conformance.test.ts`'s large-backlog case over it, asserting the SAME invariants on every arm — the returned window is the oldest `limit` after `since` (or the newest `limit` when sinceless), `nextCursor` equals the last returned message's cursor, and repeated drains lose nothing. `fixture-fidelity.test.ts` is too narrow to have caught this: it asserts the request BODY on the wire and the page COUNT, never a property of the response the walk actually branches on.

summary: `requireUsableMap('mention_map', 'a handle', …)` accepts any non-empty string, but a `mention_map` value has exactly one job: it is substituted for `<@U…>` so that core's `parseMentions` reads it back as `@handle`. A value core itself would refuse as an identity handle (core's `isMentionableHandle` / `config.ts:213` refuses one for `identity.handle` under `mention_filter`) loads without complaint and then silently fails to do the only thing the map exists for. The plugin's own docstring says this map is validated fail-fast "so that a blank or non-string value cannot … cross the seam as an empty senderHandle" — it stops one step short of the value's purpose.
failure: Reproduced: `mention_map: { U0BOSS: "@alice" }`, inbound Slack text `<@U0BOSS> please review` → `Message.content` = `"@@alice please review"`, `Message.mentions` = `[]`. With `live_push.mention_filter: true` every message mentioning that user is dropped. `mention_map: { U0BOSS: "team lead" }` → content `"@team lead please review"`, `mentions` = `['team']` — never the configured handle. Both configs `connect()` successfully with no warning.
remediation: Validate each `mention_map` value at load against the round trip it must satisfy: reject unless `parseMentions('@' + value)[0] === value` (`parseMentions` is exported from `@sharptrick/parley-core`, so no core change is needed and the seam stays intact). Name the key, the value, and the reason — that the rewritten markup would not parse back as a mention — the way the timer/token rejections already do.
testUpgrade: Guard the CLASS "a `backend_config` value whose TYPE is valid but whose PURPOSE is unachievable": extend `hostile-input.test.ts`'s `CONFIG_MAPS` × `UNUSABLE_TARGETS` table with a purpose axis generated from `parseMentions` — a row set of handles that are non-empty strings yet not round-trippable (`'@alice'`, `'team lead'`, `'bob!'`, `'-lead'`, `'x.'`, an emoji) asserted to be refused at `connect`, plus round-trippable rows asserted to load AND to appear in `Message.mentions` after an inbound `<@U…>`. The existing rows only vary emptiness and JS type, so no row could ever have reached this.

summary: `blockForMessage` arms a waiter, then `await this.runFetch(...)`. If that re-query rejects (a transient Slack `ok:false`, a 5xx, a `SlackShapeError`), the rejection propagates straight out of `fetchRecent` and neither `wake()` nor `await wait` is ever reached — the waiter stays registered in `link.waiters` with a live timer, and is iterated by every subsequent live event on that channel until its own rung timer (up to `MAX_DIAL_BACKOFF_MS` = 5 s) fires. `harness.ts`'s `parkedWaiters` docstring names exactly this class, but every assertion of it in the suite sits on the resolved arm, so the rejection arm is ungraded.
failure: Reproduced: `fetchRecent({topic, since: asCursor('0'), blockMs: 4000})` with `conversations.history` made to answer `ok:false, internal_error` 300 ms into the block. The call rejects with `SlackApiError: Slack conversations.history → internal_error`, and `parkedWaiters(plugin)` immediately after the rejection is `1` (expected `0`).
remediation: Make the waiter's lifetime match the call's, not the timer's: wrap the re-query so the waiter is released on every exit — e.g. `try { const requeried = await this.runFetch(...); … } finally { wake(); }` with the `await wait` moved to the empty-result branch, or arm it under a `using`-style disposer. A rejected call must leave the registry exactly as it found it.
testUpgrade: Guard the CLASS "a resource armed before a fallible step and released only on success": parameterize the blocking-fetch suite over an OUTCOME axis — resolved-with-messages, resolved-empty-at-deadline, rejected mid-block (injected `ok:false`, injected 500, injected malformed body), and rejected on the entry read — and assert `parkedWaiters(plugin) === 0` on every arm, not only where the call resolves. The `DEGRADATIONS × LANDING_FRACTIONS` table is too narrow: every one of its 30 rows ends in a successful read.

summary: `seam.ts` states as a contract that "`subscribe`'s handler is invoked in ascending order" per topic, and the conformance suite grades it — but only on one stable connection. On a `disconnect: warning` the plugin deliberately runs two Socket Mode connections for up to `rotation_grace_ms` (default 10 s), Slack routes each payload to exactly one of them, and `routeEnvelope` contains no ordering logic whatsoever: whichever socket's TCP stream delivers first wins. The plugin therefore knowingly suspends an explicit seam guarantee on every routine Slack refresh; the exposure is stated in a source comment and in `connection-lifecycle.test.ts:500`, but nowhere an operator reads — the README's Socket Mode row says only "one shared websocket per plugin instance".
failure: Rotation overlap: events E1 (ts 100.000001) routed by Slack to the OLD connection and E2 (ts 100.000002) routed to the NEW one. With independent TCP paths, E2 can arrive first; `routeEnvelope` invokes the handler with E2 then E1 — descending `ts`, violating the seam's ascending-order clause. Nothing in the plugin detects or corrects it, and no test in the package covers ordering while `liveSockets === 2`.
remediation: Enforce the guarantee the seam states rather than resting it on a property Slack explicitly does not promise: keep a per-channel `lastDeliveredTs` in the link and deliver only events strictly after it, letting a straggler be recovered by cursor catch-up (which already owns every gap). If the exposure is instead accepted, state it in the README where an operator reads — that live delivery order is only guaranteed while one connection feeds a channel, and that a rotation opens a `rotation_grace_ms` window where it is not.
testUpgrade: Guard the CLASS "a seam guarantee that holds only in the plugin's steady state": add a rotation-overlap ordering case that opens the grace (`pushUnackedEnvelope({type:'disconnect', reason:'warning'})`, wait for `liveSockets === 2`), then pushes a ts-ascending run of events across BOTH sockets in adversarial arrival order (a `FakeSlack` helper that targets a chosen socket), and asserts the handler saw them in ascending `ts`. Parameterize over the socket-count states already enumerated in `SOCKET_STATES` so the invariant is graded in every state the plugin can hold more than one event source, not only the steady one.

summary: `validateConfig` checks each token's TYPE but never its presence, and `connect()` succeeds with no `bot_token` at all. Every Web API call then omits the `Authorization` header entirely and comes back `not_authed`. This is exactly inverted from the optional credential: the plugin has a deliberate, named fail-fast for a missing `app_token` ("Slack Socket Mode needs an app_token; this deployment has no live push", `link.ts:102`), which is legitimately optional for a reactive-only deployment — while the one credential with no legal absence is unchecked.
failure: Reproduced: `plugin.connect({ api_url, app_token: 'xapp-test' })` resolves, `cli.ts` prints `parley-slack: bridge up`, and then `post` → `SlackApiError: Slack chat.postMessage → not_authed`, `fetchRecent` → `Slack conversations.history → not_authed`, `subscribe` → `Slack conversations.history → not_authed`, `resolveIdentity` → `Slack auth.test → not_authed`. Not one of the four errors names `bot_token` or `backend_config`.
remediation: Reject a missing (or empty) `bot_token` in `resolveConfig`, in the same shape as the other load errors — `Slack backend_config.bot_token is required: every Web API call (chat.postMessage, conversations.history, users.lookupByEmail, auth.test) is sent as Bearer <bot_token>`. Keep it a load error, so an operator learns at start rather than on the first tool call.
testUpgrade: Guard the CLASS "a `backend_config` credential the plugin cannot function without": drive the token table in `hostile-input.test.ts` off `TOKEN_CONFIG_KEYS` plus a per-key REQUIRED flag, with rows for absent / `''` / whitespace-only, asserting a load error naming the key for every required credential and a documented, named runtime refusal for every optional one. Today's table only varies the type of a token that IS present (`42`, `true`, `null`, `{}`, `['xoxb-test']`), so absence has no row anywhere.

summary: A single malformed `GET /users/@me` 200 permanently poisons the `resolveIdentity` memo: the shape is never checked, the failure happens outside the memo's catch, and every later call re-throws an opaque TypeError without re-requesting.
failure: Discord (or a CDN/proxy in front of it) answers `GET /users/@me` with `200 null`. Reproduced against test/fake-discord.ts: call 0 -> `TypeError: Cannot read properties of null (reading 'username')`, call 1 -> same error, call 2 -> same error, with `/users/@me` request count stuck at 1 for the life of the connection. The memo's `.catch` ("don't cache a transient failure") never runs, because `this.me` RESOLVED — it is `me.username` in the caller that throws. The `200 {}` variant is quieter and worse: the bot's own handle silently resolves to `backendRef: handle` instead of its real snowflake, memoized forever, so core can never map the bot to its Discord id. Only a reconnect clears it.
remediation: Give `/users/@me` the same treatment `hasUsableId` / `pageRecords` / `dispatchedMessage` / `heartbeatIntervalOf` already give every other provider body: validate `{ id: non-empty string, username: non-empty string }` inside the memoized chain and reject with a Discord-named error there, so the existing `this.me = undefined` catch fires and the next call retries. Same for `resolveUrl`'s `{ url }` and `unpushableReason`'s `{ type }`.
testUpgrade: CLASS: a seam call that casts a provider 200 without checking it. Lift the existing `describe('a malformed 200 from the provider')` table in test/rest-contract.test.ts from a fetchRecent/post table to a table over EVERY seam call that parses a REST body — cross `[resolveIdentity, subscribe(channel check), gateway url resolution, fetchRecent, post]` against `[null, 'a string', 42, [], {}, {id:1,username:2}]` (the fake needs `rawBody: 'null'`, since `injectFault` currently normalizes `body: null` to `{}` via `fault.body ?? {}` and cannot express it). Assert per cell: the call either succeeds with well-typed values or rejects with an Error whose message contains 'Discord', AND that a subsequent identical call re-issues the HTTP request (`requestCount` strictly increases) — that second clause is what catches the memo poisoning and would keep catching it wherever a memo is added next.

summary: `newestWindow` interpolates a provider-supplied message id straight into the `before=` query parameter, while `windowSince` escapes the same class of value with `encodeURIComponent` — so a hostile or corrupted page body can inject parameters into the plugin's next authenticated request.
failure: A `GET /channels/<id>/messages` page whose oldest record carries `id: "100000000000001&after=0&limit=3"` makes the backward walk issue, with the bot token attached, `GET /api/v10/channels/740000000000000103/messages?limit=100&before=100000000000001&after=0&limit=3` (observed verbatim). The injected `after=` flips Discord's windowing direction and the injected `limit=` contradicts the plugin's own, so the walk fetches a window it never asked for; a `#` in the id truncates the query entirely. `windowSince` (catchup.ts:29) already does `encodeURIComponent(last ?? since)` for the identical value, so this is a one-sided gap, not a considered choice — and the package otherwise treats provider bodies as untrusted (see the 'malformed 200 from the provider' table).
remediation: `before=${encodeURIComponent(before)}` in `newestWindow`, matching `windowSince`. Better: have `walk` escape the anchor once before handing it to the `query` callback, so neither orientation can be written unescaped again.
testUpgrade: CLASS: provider-controlled data reaching a request URL unescaped. Add a parameterized case in test/paging-contract.test.ts driving BOTH walk directions (`no since` / `since`) with an injected page whose anchor record's id is drawn from a table of hostile shapes — `'1&limit=1'`, `'1&after=0'`, `'1#x'`, `'1 2'`, `'1%2F..%2F'`, `'1/../../users/@me'` — and assert on `fake.requests()` that every issued `/messages` URL has exactly one `limit` and at most one of `before`/`after`, and that its path is still `/api/v10/channels/<topic>/messages`. Widen the same generator over `post`'s `inReplyTo` and any future id-derived query. The existing malformed-200 table cannot catch this: it only inspects the RESULT, never the requests the walk emitted.

summary: `handshake_timeout_ms` is accepted unvalidated: `0`, a negative, or a non-number permanently disables live push with nothing but a per-attempt stderr warn — while the sibling knob `gateway_dialers` fails fast at `connect()` for exactly the same class of value.
failure: `backend_config: { handshake_timeout_ms: 0 }` (which a reasonable operator reads as 'no timeout', the POSIX/`SO_TIMEOUT` convention). Reproduced: `connect()` resolves, `subscribe()` RESOLVES (a stalled handshake is classified transient), one stderr line `live push for topic "..." is not up yet (Discord gateway handshake timed out after 0ms (no READY)); the reconnect ladder is retrying`, and then zero messages are ever pushed — `setTimeout(..., 0)` fires before any HELLO can arrive, so every dial on the ladder is terminated at once, forever, climbing to the 120s ceiling. The bridge looks healthy: catch-up and `post` work, `parley-discord: bridge up — live_push=true` is printed, and there is no further diagnostic. `NaN` and a negative behave identically (both coerce to 0 in `setTimeout`).
remediation: Add `requireHandshakeTimeout(value)` alongside `requireDistinctChannels` / `requireReconnectCap` in config.ts and call it from `connect()`: reject anything that is not an integer >= some floor (the handshake is at minimum a network round trip), naming the value the way `requireReconnectCap` does.
testUpgrade: CLASS: a numeric backend_config knob with no validation, where an out-of-range value degrades a half of the bridge instead of failing the load. Generalize the existing `BAD_DIALERS = [0, -1, 1.5]` table in test/gateway-budget.test.ts into a table over KNOBS x BAD VALUES — `['gateway_dialers','handshake_timeout_ms'] x [0, -1, 1.5, NaN, 'x', null]` — asserting `connect()` rejects with a message naming the key. Pair it with a positive control per knob (a sane value connects and reaches READY) so the table cannot pass by refusing everything, and extend it whenever a knob is added; that is what would have caught this one, since `handshake_timeout_ms` simply was not on the axis.

summary: An ordinary Discord 429 whose hint exceeds the long-poll's own (small) budget rejects `fetchRecent`, because `fetchWithin` only answers the safe empty page when the deadline has ALREADY passed — but a fast 429 fails long before that.
failure: `fetchRecent({ topic, since, limit: 10, blockMs: 2000 })` while Discord answers one 429 with `retry_after: 3` (3 s — a routine per-route bucket wait). Reproduced: the call rejects after 15 ms with `HttpStatusError: Discord GET /channels/.../messages?after=1&limit=10 → 429: upstream asked for 3000ms, past this call's 1990ms deadline (4ms elapsed)`. `fetchWithin` rethrows because `Date.now() < walk.deadline`. Core's blocking wrapper calls the plugin repeatedly for one tool call, so the model gets an `isError` tool result for a transient rate limit on a call whose entire contract is 'return possibly empty and let core poll the rest of its budget' — the exact reasoning the code comment at index.ts:104-106 gives for returning early/empty. The smaller the `block_ms`, the more ordinary a 429 has to be to trigger it; core's 250 ms poll fallback makes almost any hint fatal.
remediation: In `fetchWithin`, answer the empty replayable page for a RETRYABLE rate-limit failure regardless of the clock (keep the existing rule that `NoSuchTopicError` and non-429 failures propagate), so a 429 costs the long-poll its remaining budget rather than the tool call. The deadline-only condition is what makes the swallow unreachable for the fast case.
testUpgrade: CLASS: a transient/retryable backend failure surfacing as a hard error from a call whose contract permits an empty answer. Parameterize a case over `blockMs in [0, 250, 2000, 60000]` x `retry_after in [0.5, 3, 30, 120]` x `[since, no since]`, asserting: (a) a 429 the call could not have waited out yields either an empty result with `nextCursor === since` or an error, and (b) for every cell with `blockMs > 0` it is the empty result, and (c) `NoSuchTopicError` and a 500 still propagate in every cell (the negative control that stops the table passing on a plugin that swallows everything). The existing readme.test.ts 429 case pins only the no-blockMs path against `DEFAULT_DEADLINE_MS`, so it cannot see this.

summary: The '## Rate limits (429)' table states the failure threshold as 'a hint longer than the call's remaining budget (**30000 ms**)' — but on the read path that table is written for, the budget is `block_ms` (floored at 250 ms per page), not 30000 ms.
failure: An operator reads the table and sizes their bot's load on the premise that Discord hints under 30 s are waited out. In fact `fetchRecent({ blockMs: 2000 })` fails on a 3 s hint (reproduced above), and `fetchRecent({ blockMs: 1 })` fails on anything over ~250 ms, because `pager` passes `deadlineMs: budgetMs` from the walk (index.ts:162, catchup.ts:69) instead of net-util's default. 30000 ms is only ever the budget for `post`, `resolveIdentity`, the channel check and `GET /gateway/bot`. The operator advice that follows ('reduce the load on the bot token ... rather than to wait the limit out') is derived from the wrong threshold.

summary: StoreLock.claim() clears a stale claim with a bare unlinkSync, so two starters that both observed the SAME dead pid each delete the other's fresh claim and both end up holding the store file — the exact 'two writers on one observed-message store' state the class doc calls structurally unsupported.

A resumes, unlinkSync removes B's claim, tryClaim succeeds. `a.claim()` returns instead of throwing; both A and B have held=true. Also: whichever releases first unlinks the survivor's claim, so a third bridge then joins too.
remediation: Make the replacement atomic or verifiable: write the pid to a unique sibling (`<path>.lock.<pid>.<rand>`) and `linkSync` it into place (link is atomic and fails EEXIST), or — minimally — after a successful post-unlink tryClaim, re-read the lock file and abort unless it names this process, so the loser of the race detects it lost. The existing `FOREIGN_CLAIMS` table only exercises a serial claim against a pre-written lock, so no row can ever have two claimants in flight.

summary: The `#seq <issued> <intact>` watermark can never detect a TAIL rollback of the append-only store file: a truncation/restore that drops the newest records drops their watermark lines with them, so `intact === onDisk`, the epoch is NOT re-minted, and the store re-issues sequences an agent is still holding — cursor `<epoch>.N` silently names a different message.
failure: Reproduced (vitest probe, now removed): ObservedStore appends m1..m3, snapshot the file (whole, newline-terminated — i.e. an ordinary backup), append m4,m5, agent holds cursor `E.4`; restore the snapshot; reload. Observed `restored.epoch() === E` (README says a fresh identity is minted) and `highWater() === 3`. The next append returns seq 4, so `E.4` now names 'a different message'. `requireOwnCursor` then accepts `E.4` (4 <= highWater) and `fetchRecent({since:'E.4'})` filters `seq > 4`, so the new message is never delivered to that agent and is never reported — on the one backend where no history endpoint can backfill it. README 'History limitations' claims exactly this class is caught ('A file partially rolled back — same identity, records missing — is caught the same way'), and assigns the residual only to files 'written before that watermark existed'.
remediation: Persist the issued high-water where a rollback of the JSONL alone cannot take it with the records — e.g. a sibling `<store_path>.hw` (or the lock file) rewritten on append, compared at load: a sidecar above the loaded high-water means records were lost, so mint a fresh identity. The current `cursor-lifecycle` cells only cut mid-line (which trips the torn-tail path) or use a pre-watermark file, so no row exercises a boundary-aligned tail loss.

summary: pollUpdates advances `offset` for every update in the batch before `deliver` runs, so an update whose store append THREW or was refused is acknowledged to Telegram on the next poll and permanently lost — even though the ~24h getUpdates backlog is the only redelivery this backend has and the store is the only history it can ever produce.
